articles.title: Does stress, anger, or sadness drive you to eat
articles.fallbackTitle: Does stress, anger, or sadness drive you to eat

blocks.text: Does stress, anger, or sadness drive you to eat? Do you turn to food for comfort, or when you’re bored? Many people do. If you often eat for emotional reasons instead of because you’re physically hungry, that can be a problem.
blocks.translation: 压力、愤怒或悲伤会驱使你吃东西吗？你会不会在寻求安慰或无聊时转向食物？许多人都这样。如果你经常因为情绪原因而进食，而不是因为身体饥饿，那可能是个问题。

blocks.text: Obeying the urge to eat more than you need is certain to gain weight. It’s an even bigger problem if you already have health conditions like high blood pressure.
blocks.translation: 屈服从多吃一点的冲动，必然会导致体重增加。如果你已经有高血压等健康问题，那就更是个大问题。

blocks.text: You can get back in control of your emotional eating. The surprising part is, it’s not really about food at all. The solution to emotional eating is less about eating than it is about emotions. You can start with a simple step. “Make a list of what is stressing you, and make a plan to take control of the situation,” New York psychologist Patricia Farrell says. If you can change the situation, go for it. If the problem is out of your control, you can manage the way you think about it. If you can notice your stress in the moment, you can choose how you respond, rather than reacting the way you have in the past. It helps to add a delay between the urge to eat and the actual eating. That gives you time to check in with how you’re feeling and why you want to eat.
blocks.translation: 你可以重新控制情绪化进食。令人惊讶的是，这其实与食物无关。解决情绪化进食，与其说关乎吃，不如说关乎情绪。你可以从一个简单的步骤开始。纽约心理学家帕特里夏·法雷尔说：“列出让你有压力的事情，并制定一个控制局面的计划。”如果你能改变现状，就去做。如果问题超出你的控制，你可以调整自己对它的看法。如果你能在当下察觉自己的压力，你就能选择如何回应，而不是像过去那样做出反应。在进食冲动和真正进食之间加一段延迟会有帮助，这让你有时间审视自己的感受以及想吃东西的原因。

blocks.text: When you get the urge to eat a cookie out of sadness or boredom, remember that you have the choice to wait it out. “Tell yourself to have it later,” Farrell says. Even if it doesn’t, successfully delaying the snack helps you feel more in control.
blocks.translation: 当你因为悲伤或无聊而想吃一块饼干时，记住你可以选择等一等。“告诉自己晚点再吃，”法雷尔说。即使最后没吃，成功推迟这份零食也会让你感到更有掌控感。

blocks.text: In addition, consider talking with a doctor so you can better understand what’s going on with you and the best way to handle it.
blocks.translation: 此外，考虑咨询医生，以便更好地了解自己的状况以及最好的应对方法。

paragraphs: Does stress, anger, or sadness drive you to eat? Do you turn to food for comfort, or when you’re bored? Many people do. If you often eat for emotional reasons instead of because you’re physically hungry, that can be a problem.
Obeying the urge to eat more than you need is certain to gain weight. It’s an even bigger problem if you already have health conditions like high blood pressure.

You can get back in control of your emotional eating. The surprising part is, it’s not really about food at all. The solution to emotional eating is less about eating than it is about emotions. You can start with a simple step. “Make a list of what is stressing you, and make a plan to take control of the situation,” New York psychologist Patricia Farrell says. If you can change the situation, go for it. If the problem is out of your control, you can manage the way you think about it. If you can notice your stress in the moment, you can choose how you respond, rather than reacting the way you have in the past. It helps to add a delay between the urge to eat and the actual eating. That gives you time to check in with how you’re feeling and why you want to eat.

When you get the urge to eat a cookie out of sadness or boredom, remember that you have the choice to wait it out. “Tell yourself to have it later,” Farrell says. Even if it doesn’t, successfully delaying the snack helps you feel more in control.
In addition, consider talking with a doctor so you can better understand what’s going on with you and the best way to handle it.

articles.title: A new study shows that plants are creating frequencies in responses to their surroundings,
articles.fallbackTitle: A new study shows that plants are creating frequencies in responses to their surroundings,

blocks.text: A new study shows that plants are creating frequencies in responses to their surroundings, or in other words, they are reacting. These “reactions” in plants, which we could see as analogous to human senses, are actually nothing new. We have learned over the past few years that plants are capable of seeing, hearing, and smelling.
blocks.translation: 一项新研究表明，植物会因应周围环境产生不同频率，换句话说，它们在做反应。植物这些“反应”可以看作类似人类的感官，其实并不新鲜。过去几年我们已经了解到，植物能够看见、听见和闻到。

blocks.text: And with this newest finding we are just one sense away from completing the five human senses in some plants. For the first time, plants have been recorded making airborne sounds when stressed, which researchers say could open up a new field of precision agriculture where farmers listen for water starved crops.
blocks.translation: 有了这项最新发现，我们在某些植物身上只差一种感官就能凑齐人类的五种感官。研究人员首次记录到植物在受压时发出空气传播的声音，他们说这可能开辟精准农业的新领域，让农民通过“听”来发现缺水的作物。

blocks.text: The researchers found that tomato and tobacco plants made sounds at frequencies humans cannot hear when facing situations such as lack of water or when being cut.
blocks.translation: 研究人员发现，番茄和烟草植物在缺水或被切割等情况下，会发出人类听不到的声音频率。

blocks.text: On average, drought-stressed tomato plants made 35 sounds per hour, while tobacco plants made 11 and unstressed plants produced fewer than one sound per hour.
blocks.translation: 平均而言，受干旱胁迫的番茄植株每小时发出 35 个声音，烟草植株发出 11 个，而未受胁迫的植株每小时发出的声音不到一个。

blocks.text: The researchers trained a machine-learning model to tell difference between the plant’s sounds and the wind, rain, and other surrounding noises of the greenhouse, in order to correctly identify the source of stress. Results showed that drought-stressed plants make significantly more sounds than control plants.
blocks.translation: 研究人员训练了一个机器学习模型，用来区分植物的声音与风、雨以及温室中其他环境噪音，从而正确识别压力来源。结果显示，受干旱胁迫的植物发出的声音明显多于对照植物。

blocks.text: Humans cannot hear the whole range of frequencies around us. If we could, we would likely become absent-minded and anxious by always hearing the frequencies around us including radio frequencies from cell towers near us or even cooking a frozen meal in the microwave. Thankfully, the range of human hearing is typically considered to be only 20 Hz to 20, 000 Hz. That is why humans are not sensitive to the sounds that plants are making.
blocks.translation: 人类无法听到周围所有的频率范围。如果能听到，我们大概会变得心不在焉、焦虑不安，因为会一直听到周围的各种频率，包括附近手机基站的无线电频率，甚至用微波炉加热冷冻食品时的频率。所幸，人类的听觉范围通常被认为只有 20 赫兹到 20,000 赫兹。这就是人类对植物发出的声音不敏感的原因。

paragraphs: A new study shows that plants are creating frequencies in responses to their surroundings, or in other words, they are reacting. These “reactions” in plants, which we could see as analogous to human senses, are actually nothing new. We have learned over the past few years that plants are capable of seeing, hearing, and smelling.

And with this newest finding we are just one sense away from completing the five human senses in some plants. For the first time, plants have been recorded making airborne sounds when stressed, which researchers say could open up a new field of precision agriculture where farmers listen for water starved crops.
The researchers found that tomato and tobacco plants made sounds at frequencies humans cannot hear when facing situations such as lack of water or when being cut.
On average, drought-stressed tomato plants made 35 sounds per hour, while tobacco plants made 11 and unstressed plants produced fewer than one sound per hour.

The researchers trained a machine-learning model to tell difference between the plant’s sounds and the wind, rain, and other surrounding noises of the greenhouse, in order to correctly identify the source of stress. Results showed that drought-stressed plants make significantly more sounds than control plants.

Humans cannot hear the whole range of frequencies around us. If we could, we would likely become absent-minded and anxious by always hearing the frequencies around us including radio frequencies from cell towers near us or even cooking a frozen meal in the microwave. Thankfully, the range of human hearing is typically considered to be only 20 Hz to 20, 000 Hz. That is why humans are not sensitive to the sounds that plants are making.

articles.title: Each year, 1.3 million people worldwide die in car accidents
articles.fallbackTitle: Each year, 1.3 million people worldwide die in car accidents

blocks.text: Each year, 1.3 million people worldwide die in car accidents. Ninety-four percent of those crashes are due to human error. This is a tragedy that self-driving vehicles can help prevent. That’s because computers can think better and react earlier than people.
blocks.translation: 每年全世界有 130 万人死于车祸。其中 94% 的事故是由人为失误造成的。这是自动驾驶汽车可以帮助避免的悲剧，因为计算机比人思考得更好、反应更早。

blocks.text: As soon as we can show that a self-driving car can drive more safely than a human, we should expect to see many more such vehicles picking up passengers across the country — and eventually around the world.
blocks.translation: 一旦我们能证明自动驾驶汽车比人类驾驶更安全，就应该会看到更多这类车辆在全国各地接送乘客——最终遍布全世界。

blocks.text: Self-driving cars will also help speed up the shift toward increased ride sharing and reduced car ownership. Many people already use ride-sharing services instead of owning their own cars. Self-driving vehicles are a great fit for ride sharing because machines have the potential to find the best routes for getting people to their destinations more safely and quickly than human drivers.
blocks.translation: 自动驾驶汽车还将有助于加快向更多拼车、减少汽车拥有量的转变。许多人已经使用拼车服务而不是自己买车。自动驾驶汽车非常适合拼车，因为机器有潜力找到最佳路线，比人类司机更安全、更快捷地把人们送到目的地。

blocks.text: A future where more of us use ride sharing as our primary mode of transportation means we’ll need fewer cars overall, which comes with key benefits, including reduced road congestion and less time wasted in traffic. Fewer cars also mean less pollution and fewer parking spaces. That would make room for more parks, bike lanes, and businesses.
blocks.translation: 未来，如果我们中更多人把拼车作为主要出行方式，就意味着总体上需要的汽车更少，这会带来重要好处，包括减少道路拥堵、减少堵车浪费的时间。汽车更少也意味着污染更少、停车位更少。这将为更多公园、自行车道和商业设施腾出空间。

blocks.text: Real-world testing is critical to getting this technology ready for nationwide use. That’s why some companies are testing self-driving cars in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and Tempe, Arizona. Both cities have welcomed this technology with open arms.
blocks.translation: 实地测试对于让这项技术做好全国推广的准备至关重要。这就是为什么一些公司正在宾夕法尼亚州匹兹堡和亚利桑那州坦佩测试自动驾驶汽车。这两座城市都张开双臂欢迎这项技术。

blocks.text: A better future is within reach. We already have the technology. While it won’t happen overnight, self-driving cars will be an important part of the future of transportation.
blocks.translation: 更美好的未来触手可及。我们已经拥有了这项技术。虽然不会一夜之间实现，但自动驾驶汽车将成为未来交通的重要组成部分。
